title: La farmacia de guardia
label: ch:es-guardia
canDo: I can get a medicine that is not in stock: ask for it by the word on the box, ask them to order it in, find out when it arrives, and find the chemist that is open tonight.

payoff.summary: Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
payoff.note: ALL THREE WORDS ARE RELATIVES OF WORDS ALREADY TAUGHT, and encargar is the clearest chain in the tranche: carrus (the cart) gave el carrito, then el cargo (a load put on a bill, ch456), then ENCARGAR -- a TASK LOADED ONTO SOMEBODY. Four lessons apart and one picture throughout, which is also why encargarse de means taking responsibility and el encargado is the person with the load on; English reached for the same metaphor in 'in charge' and 'charged with'. ENCARGAR IS NOT PEDIR: you pedir what is on the menu and encargar what has to be brought in -- pedir takes something off a list, encargar creates a job for somebody. medicamento is medicus and medēri, to heal, so el médico and el medicamento are the healer and the thing that heals; an older root behind medeor is independently supported by modus, moderate and meditate, but the lesson refuses the causal story: glossing that root as 'measure' and offering a doctor's judgement as proof argues in a circle, which ES-C394-medico (a prerequisite) says explicitly. -MENTO AND -MIENTO ARE THE SAME LATIN ENDING BY THE TWO ROADS (seguimiento/medicamento, pensamiento/documento), both masculine, and the spelling carries REGISTER rather than meaning: -miento everyday, -mento formal. la guardia is Germanic wardōn, the root of guardar, and Spanish gu- regularly answers English w- (guardar/ward, guerra/war), with English guard being the same Germanic word arriving back by way of French. ONE WORD, TWO GENDERS, TWO MEANINGS: la guardia is the watch and el guardia is the officer keeping it, and the pattern is consistent -- feminine for the abstract thing, masculine for the person (la guía/el guía, la policía/el policía).
